query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, pre‐formed Al₂O₃ coating via physical vapor deposition on a refractory high‐entropy alloy will promote the in situ development of a continuous, protective alumina scale that substantially reduces high-temperature oxidation compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high‐entropy alloy that, in its untreated form, forms non-protective or discontinuous oxide scales under extreme oxygen exposures.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin pre‐formed Al₂O₃ coating on the alloy surface using a technique such as physical vapor deposition.
generation.conditions: Exposure at ~1150°C in a 1 atm oxygen-rich atmosphere for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent Al₂O₃ layer that acts as a diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: The pre‐formed Al₂O₃ coating seeds the formation of a robust, slow-growing oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby slowing down oxygen ingress and reducing oxidation kinetics by limiting further scale growth and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in oxidation rate (mass gain) and improved integrity of the oxide scale relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high‐entropy alloy, which forms non-protective, discontinuous oxide layers under the same high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under extreme thermal oxidation conditions (approximately 1150°C, 1 atm O₂, 100-hour exposure); performance outside these conditions remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding the long-term adhesion and mechanical stability of the pre‐formed coating under thermal cycling and potential differences in substrate/coating coefficient of thermal expansion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA specimens with identical composition and processing history. Apply a thin, pre‐formed Al₂O₃ coating to one set using physical vapor deposition while leaving the other set untreated. Expose both sets to a 1 atm oxygen-rich atmosphere at 1150°C for 100 hours. After exposure, analyze the samples by measuring mass gain (mg/cm²) and performing microstructural characterization (e.g., scanning electron microscopy) to assess oxide scale continuity and adhesion.
measurements: Mass gain (mg/cm²) as an indicator of oxidation rate
Oxide scale morphology and continuity by microscopy
Coating adhesion and presence of spallation or cracks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al₂O₃-coated specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., at least 25% lower mass gain) in oxidation rate and maintain a continuous, adherent oxide scale compared to the untreated specimens, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties

frame.system: Refractory high‐entropy alloys intended for structural applications at extreme temperatures; these alloys in their original state lack a robust, protective oxide scale when exposed to high-temperature oxygen environments.
frame.goal: Improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of the alloy by promoting the in situ formation of a stable, continuous, protective oxide scale that minimizes further oxidation.
frame.limitation: The untreated alloy forms nonprotective or discontinuous oxide scales at extreme temperatures, which leads to accelerated oxidation and deterioration.
constraints: Only a single intervention can be applied

The hypothesis must include a mechanism explanation, predicted improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defined test conditions (temperature, atmosphere, exposure duration), citation of prior evidence, and an experimental design with a clear, falsifying result
frame.regime: High-temperature oxidation conditions, for example, exposure at approximately 1150°C in an oxygen-rich environment (1 atm O2) for a prolonged duration (e.g., 100 hours)
prior_attempts: Previous alloying attempts (using multi-element modifications) or surface treatments that either did not form a continuous protective scale or required complex multi-step processing, thus failing to reliably improve oxidation resistance under extreme conditions.

decision.trend: Over recent years, studies on refractory high‐entropy alloys have focused on understanding their oxidation kinetics and the effects of alloying modifications. Early work measured how untreated alloys (such as AlNbTiVZr‐based systems) develop nonprotective, discontinuous oxide scales at intermediate temperatures, while later studies (e.g., via controlled Cr additions in WVTaTiCrₓ systems) refined microstructures and subtly altered scale formation. However, while composition tweaks have been attempted, they have not reliably triggered the autonomous, in situ formation of a continuous, slow-growing protective oxide layer under extreme oxidation conditions.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved challenge is to achieve a robust and adherent oxide scale that can withstand prolonged exposure at extreme temperatures (around 1150°C in 1 atm oxygen) without undergoing breakaway oxidation. Alloying interventions alone have not consistently promoted the formation of such a protective scale.
decision.lever: Apply a thin, pre‐formed Al₂O₃ coating (via techniques such as physical vapor deposition or controlled pre-oxidation) to the HEA surface
decision.why: Given that refractory HEAs inherently fail to develop a continuous protective scale through intrinsic composition changes, engineering the surface to pre-establish an alumina layer leverages the well-known high-temperature stability and oxygen barrier properties of Al₂O₃. This single intervention directly seeds a protective oxide that is expected to grow in situ under exposure at ~1150°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere, providing a clear experimental route that builds on prior evidence and addresses the observed limitations in untreated alloys.
